name: Library and Archival Systems
region: Global (Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, India, China, Islamic world, Europe, Mesoamerica)
summary: Organized institutions for collecting, cataloguing, preserving, and providing access to recorded knowledge — from Sumerian tablet archives to the House of Wisdom to modern digital repositories — the filesystem that makes accumulated knowledge retrievable.

claims.statement: Curated archives enabled knowledge accumulation across generations by preventing loss, organizing retrieval, and standardizing cataloguing — creating institutional memory that outlives individuals

The Islamic House of Wisdom and translation movement systematically preserved and transmitted Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge that would otherwise have been lost, demonstrating libraries as cross-cultural knowledge bridges
Library systems emerged independently in Mesopotamia, China, Mesoamerica, and India, converging on similar organizational principles (cataloguing, classification, controlled access)

evidence.source: Pedersén (1998) Archives and Libraries in the Ancient Near East 1500–300 BC, CDL Press
Casson (2001) Libraries in the Ancient World, Yale University Press
Gutas (1998) Greek Thought, Arabic Culture: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement in Baghdad, Routledge
al-Nadim (987 CE) Kitab al-Fihrist (The Catalogue), translation by Dodge (1970), Columbia University Press
Lerner (2009) The Story of Libraries: From the Invention of Writing to the Computer Age, 2nd ed., Continuum
Robson (2019) Ancient Knowledge Networks: A Social Geography of Cuneiform Scholarship, UCL Press

notes: The convergence point of all knowledge media. Living systems, monuments, writing, and paper all need a library to become retrievable at scale. Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (668–627 BCE) was deliberately comprehensive — he ordered copies of every text in the empire. The same impulse drives the Internet Archive today. Note the moderate decentralization score (0.55): libraries concentrate knowledge, which enables both preservation and censorship. Monastery scriptoria saved classical texts through the European Dark Ages; the burning of the Library of Alexandria and the House of Wisdom destroyed irreplaceable knowledge. The medium is durable; the institution is fragile.
